fact: Lice glue their eggs to hair with a cement so strong that ordinary shampoo won't budge it.
baby: The embryo has just burrowed into the lining of the womb. The placenta and amniotic sac are starting to form.
vs: A hard little case called a nit
No shell, just a ball of cells

fact: A flea can jump around a hundred times its own body length.
baby: The neural tube, which becomes the brain and spinal cord, is forming. So is a tiny tube that will become the heart.
vs: A long tube along its back
A tiny tube, about to start beating

fact: A tick can feed on blood for days and grow more than a hundred times heavier.
baby: A tiny heart has started beating, often visible on an early scan. Little buds that will become arms and legs pop up.
vs: Hooks into skin with a barbed mouth
Through little holes in its body
Not at all. Oxygen comes from the parent's blood

fact: Carpenter ants chew tunnels through wood and happily move into the walls of your house.
baby: The brain is growing fast. Arm and leg buds are getting longer and the face is starting to take shape.
vs: Arm and leg buds, getting longer
Lives in a colony of thousands

fact: Unlike a honeybee, a wasp can sting you again and again.
baby: Fingers and toes are forming, still webbed like a frog. The little tail at the bottom is shrinking away.
vs: Builds one from chewed-up wood paper
Forming, still webbed like a frog

fact: Female horseflies slice your skin open with scissor-like mouthparts and lap up the blood.
baby: Tiny muscles are forming and the first wriggles begin, far too small to feel. Eyelids are on their way.

fact: A cockroach can survive for days without its head.
baby: All the major organs are in place and now just need to grow. From here on it's officially a fetus.
vs: One of the fastest insects on foot

fact: When threatened, millipedes ooze a foul-smelling fluid.
baby: Fingers and toes have separated. Tooth buds are hiding in the gums.
vs: 4, with separate fingers and toes now
Tooth buds forming in the gums

fact: Stag beetle larvae can live in rotting wood for up to six years before they grow up.
baby: Reflexes are kicking in: fingers open and close and the mouth makes sucking movements. Often time for the first scan.
vs: Can open and close the mouth

fact: Every Spanish slug is both male and female, and each one can lay hundreds of eggs.
baby: Vocal cords are forming. The head is still huge, but the body is starting to catch up.
vs: Litres of it, over a lifetime
Floats in fluid, but stays clean
Thousands of tiny teeth on its tongue

fact: A medicinal leech has three jaws with around a hundred tiny teeth on each.
baby: Can squint, frown and pull faces. Fine, fuzzy hair called lanugo starts to grow all over.
vs: A big blood meal, then months of fasting

fact: A mouse can squeeze through a gap about as narrow as a pencil.
baby: Bones are hardening. Light may already be sensed through closed eyelids.
vs: May sense it through closed eyelids

fact: Toads ooze poison from two big glands just behind their eyes.
baby: Movements are getting more coordinated. Some people feel the first flutters around now.
vs: Not yet. Oxygen comes through the cord
Pushes food down with its eyeballs

fact: Scorpions glow blue-green under UV light.
baby: Fat is starting to build up under the skin, and soft cartilage is turning into bone.
vs: Carries its young on its back
Will be carried in someone's arms

fact: African giant millipedes can grow up to 38 cm long.
baby: The ears are in place and may start picking up sounds. Movements can feel like bubbles or flutters.
vs: Gains more every time it moults
Ears in place, starting to hear
Curls up too, the classic fetal position

fact: Some stick insects can have babies without any help from a male.
baby: A waxy, cheese-like coating called vernix starts covering the skin, protecting it from all that fluid.
vs: No regrowing, so handle with care
Sways like a twig in the wind

fact: A rat's teeth never stop growing, so it has to keep gnawing its whole life.
baby: Halfway! Swallowing amniotic fluid and making meconium, the first very sticky poop. Often time for the big scan.
vs: The first poop is building up inside

fact: It can flick itchy hairs off its abdomen at anything that bothers it.
baby: Kicks are getting stronger, and sleep and wake patterns are developing.
vs: Sheds its whole skin to grow
Keeps the same skin, it just stretches

fact: Giant centipedes hang from cave ceilings and snatch bats out of the air.
baby: Eyebrows and eyelashes are growing. Grabbing the umbilical cord is a favourite hobby.
vs: Yes, from claws by its head

fact: Hedgehogs sometimes lather their own foamy spit all over their spines.
baby: Rapid eye movements have started, and loud sounds from the outside world can probably be heard.

fact: Pigeons make a kind of milk in their throat and throw it up for their chicks.
baby: The lungs are branching out and starting to make surfactant, which helps them work after birth.
vs: Doesn't need to. Never leaves home
Air sacs all through its body

fact: Black rats and their fleas get much of the blame for spreading the plague in the Middle Ages.
baby: Hands are fully formed and can make a fist. Hair is growing, colour and all.
vs: About as long as its body
Up to around 10 at a time

fact: Escaped farm mink have spread across Europe and are a menace to nesting seabirds.
baby: The eyes are starting to open. Breathing is practised by inhaling amniotic fluid.

fact: A slow worm looks like a snake, but it's really a legless lizard.
baby: Hiccups! Little rhythmic jerks that can sometimes be felt from the outside. The brain is very busy.

fact: Baby Komodo dragons live up in the trees for their first years so the adults don't eat them.
baby: Eyes can open, close and sense light. From here it's mostly about piling on weight.

fact: A frightened opossum plays dead and gives off a smell like rotting meat.
baby: Muscles and lungs keep maturing, and the head keeps growing to make room for the brain.
vs: Raised in a womb, then in arms

fact: The adder is the only venomous snake in Britain and Scandinavia.
baby: The brain is growing fast, and the fuzzy lanugo hair is starting to fall off.
vs: Sheds it all in one piece
Basks in the sun to warm up

fact: The anglerfish has its own fishing rod on its head that lures prey straight into its mouth.
baby: Can turn the head from side to side. Getting plumper as fat builds up.
vs: Can turn its head side to side

fact: Wolffish have huge fangs that crush sea urchins and shells.
baby: Fingernails and toenails are here. Breathing, swallowing and sucking are practised daily.

fact: Raccoons are so good with their hands they can open lids and simple latches.
baby: Bones are hardening, except the skull, which stays soft and squishy for the trip out.
vs: Often most active at night too
Soft and squishy, for the trip out

fact: European eels swim thousands of kilometres to the Sargasso Sea to spawn.
baby: The vernix coating gets thicker and the lungs are well on their way.

fact: Gulls can drink seawater and sneeze the salt out through glands above their eyes.
baby: Space is getting tight, so movements become more squirmy than kicky.

fact: For its size, it has one of the strongest bites of any mammal.
baby: Many have turned head down by now. Gaining around 30 grams a day.
vs: Eats whole carcasses, bones and all
Many are head down by now

fact: The king cobra is the world's longest venomous snake, and babies are venomous from day one.
baby: Early term from now. Practising for the outside: sucking, gripping and breathing movements.

fact: Badgers dig their own toilet pits a little way from their den.
baby: A surprisingly firm grip. The gut is stocked with meconium, ready for the first nappy.
vs: Has no idea what night is

fact: Herring gulls will happily steal the ice cream right out of your hand.
baby: Full term. Lungs and brain keep fine-tuning right up until birth.

fact: Nine-banded armadillos almost always give birth to identical quadruplets.
baby: Due date! Fully cooked. Only about 1 in 20 actually arrive on the day.
vs: Can hold its breath for about six minutes
Has been underwater for nine months
Only some kinds roll into a ball
Has been curled up for months
